lines.text: My name is Ed Piskor. I'm Jim Rugg. Jim, today we have a special guest, a Kayfabe lieutenant, somebody I had in mind when we started the channel, because there are very few people who can rub shoulders with both a Jordan Crane and a Jim Lee. You know what I'm saying? We've got a madman in the house.

We've got somebody who took Anthony Bourdain to Twizzler on television, man. We've got a dude who Howard Stern called the prince of all media and then adopted him. We've got the man with the dirty hands, David Choe. You sure? You see my ID out there? We vetted this. We took blood samples. We talked to the Japanese police,

got some fingerprints, and it is confirmed. [deadpan] You got nothing for the cosplay? I got the Raiders. All right, Dave, man, it's a crazy time right now. There's a lot of turmoil, the country is hurt, and, you know, this is a comic book podcast.

A lot of our comics reading comes from childhood. If you were in high school, age 15 or whatever, in 1992 when the first riots pop off, I think about what a little dude in Pittsburgh even knew about LA in general, and Koreans in LA in particular. And there's four things that I knew.

One, we have the Korean lady in the bodega who shoots the girl in the head, a Black girl, murders her, and gets off scot-free. We have Ice Cube's 'Black Korea.' And then we have two flicks, man, that are considered

fucking super cool classics, but the depiction of the Korean store owner in Menace II Society and Do the Right Thing as these paranoid, racist shop owners. That's all I knew growing up about Korean life in LA. And you had to grow up in that. You grew up in that situation, and that has to make a kid pretty tough.

[breaking character] Permission to get out of my Pistol cosplay? [laughing] Yeah, yeah, you live your life. I wanted to commit to staying in character, but it's very hot, and you asked me some very hot questions. So I gotta get my man bun out and, uh,

I don't know, man, you just fucking threw a lot of shit on the table right now. So let's get into it. The world is on fire right now, and at a moment like this it's like, let's definitely talk about comics. [laughs] You know, growing up in Los Angeles in the '90s. Oh God, this is such a...

The group NWA. Ice Cube went solo with Death Certificate, and I think the last track on Death Certificate was 'Black Korea.' And, you know, I'm a Korean American kid, first generation. My parents came here in their late 20s.

And I love NWA. I fucking love NWA. To have someone you look up to... and to be honest, I like Eazy-E better than Ice Cube, but Ice Cube's cool, man, I fucking love that guy. And it's a weird feeling when you look up to someone and then they write a song about killing your race, you know?

And fuck the lyrics, but I used to know it word for word, because if a song traumatized me I was like, man, that's Ice Cube saying if you follow me around your liquor store I'm gonna fucking kill you.

And then I think about the medium of comics. I grew up in LA. It's Meltdown, Golden Apple. And, you know, I talked to you for the first time like a week ago, right? And since then the world's exploded, and you go, 'Hey, I'd love to talk to you on the show.'

And for me, I haven't done interviews in a long time. Years. So the timing couldn't be more awkward. We're gonna sit down right now, and there are fucking people looting outside, like right down the street from here. And it's a trauma repetition, repetition. It's like, where did I go? You're talking about '92, I was 15

years old. That just imprinted: the world is not safe. It's not safe. Everything I know could be taken away in a moment. And so to just bury my head in fantasy, in a comic, that was it. I could talk to you guys right now for easily like 30

hours about everything comics. You guys are doing God's work, not even exaggerating. When I hear you guys name-dropping names I haven't heard in like 20 years, and talking about it like you know what it feels like...

It feels like when I was in Union Square a few years ago. I'd been in Africa, out of the country for a while, and I said, you know what, I'm back in America, I want to go see a movie. I went to the theater, I look at the marquee, and I go, is that fucking Aquaman?

One of the Justice League movies. Okay, I don't know if that's gonna be any good. Thor. Guardians of the Galaxy? You're talking about the four-for-a-dollar bin Guardians of the Galaxy, Jim Valentino, one of the worst fucking comic books ever, and it's the number one blockbuster.
And I'm sitting there in Union Square in New York City being like, did I come back to America? I get it if you make another Batman movie. I get it if you make Superman.

Guardians of the Galaxy? Horseshit. Aquaman, the worst character DC has, talks to fish. Thor, nobody reads Thor. The only time anyone was mildly interested in Thor was when there was the horse-looking motherfucker, Beta Ray Bill. But besides that, nobody reads Thor, nobody reads fucking Aquaman, nobody reads Guardians of the Galaxy, and there they are,

boom, in the fucking middle, and people know who these characters are. And I go, I think I'm living in an alternate reality right now. And that's the closest feeling I've had to listening to you guys. I was like, did these guys just talk about Wizard magazine for two hours and I was glued? This is

fucking mental. So for me, you guys are drugs right now. You want to talk to me? Fuck yeah, let's do it. Let's do it in the middle of... and this ain't the LA riots, this is like the world riots. They're fucking rioting in Berlin. It is insane.

Yeah, I could completely disassociate right now and talk about Asgard and wherever the fuck you guys want to go. Cool, let's do that. Then you bring up Wizard magazine, and in Slow Jams there's that one issue you're jerking off to with Gen 13 on the cover, and that

issue is the one that had the Kubert School article. When I was a little dude seeing that, I carried that issue around with me my entire high school life, because I'm like, this is where I'm gonna go. I reread that article a million times. In 1999 you put out Slow Jams,

and then you see my most important issue of Wizard sullied by fucking David Choe because he's jerking off to Fairchild in freefall. [laughing] It's my pleasure, man, my pleasure. I was a really horny teenager. When I see kids today, 15 years old... for me it was the same dynamic as stealing Playboys from the newsstand and then reading a comic. Those things went together.
Now it's more like, play video games all night and switch back and forth to Pornhub. So I was a super horny kid. And I have two brothers, my grandmother lived with us, and we lived in a tiny house.

So I can safely say every member of the household except my grandmother had caught me jerking off. And, I don't know, every time I say that now it's a story I can just tell and I don't get embarrassed.
But at 15 it was so shameful. It was such a painful experience. My little brother had walked in, and it was the one day he was at camp and everyone was out of the house, which was super rare.
You know how artists have that flat file, like of National Geographic, what do you call it? The morgue. Right, the morgue. I had a different name for it, but I can't...

Well, I had that for porn. I had a Yellow Pages telephone book, and I had pages of a really hot chick that someone drew in a comic book, or a lingerie thing, and I hid it in there so it just looked like a phone book. And the day the stars aligned and everyone was out

of the house, I laid every page out and I took all my clothes off. Before that it was always, you know, there's only one bathroom between three brothers. And my brother walked in, and I had never felt shame on that level. And I come from a super

religious family. Then my dad found it and confronted me, and I just felt so embarrassed. As a 15-year-old, my ability to express emotions is basically just hate or anger. There's not that much range. So to get caught jerking off by mom, dad, brother number one, brother number two, I just felt judged.

I felt embarrassed. I felt like I was gonna go to hell, and I didn't know what to do with that. So I just put it into comics. This is before I knew about the whole... I don't even know if there's a name for it, but all

the comic artists who draw their dicks and show themselves jerking off, Joe Matt, Chester Brown. I just drew it because I didn't know what else to do with it. I was so lost. I was like, I've already been humiliated, I've already been embarrassed, I don't know what else
to do with this. I'm just gonna dive into it. So I wrote the story first. I was like, how long do I really think about Fairchild from Gen 13, Campbell drawing? Not that long. Okay, write that down.
That girl today. And I just wrote down how much I jerk, with the number of seconds. Just to write that out was enough for me. It was in my journal. I was like, oh my God, it's out there.
I was able to exorcise that demon. And then I was, I don't know, 16 or 17. And I remember going to art school. I went to art school in Oakland at a place called CCAC.
I went there for a year and a half before I dropped out. And I took a creative writing class there. And I was older now, I was 21. And I found that thing,
that story I had written when I was 16. And I was like, you know, I like it when it hurts. I like shame. I'm going to read this super embarrassing thing.

And this is art school, right? So I read this story in front of the whole cast of characters from Dan Clowes's Art School Confidential. They're all there: the feminist, the lesbian, the Conan-looking guy.
They're all there. And I'm sitting there going, 'and I jerked off to you for like 30 seconds.' And I'm ready for my mom and dad to be like, you're going to hell.

And I get, [applauding] bravo, bravo. And I go, what? This is crazy. I'm getting applauded for writing about the most shameful experience of my life. And so, as someone young and insecure and not sure of the world,

I said, wow, I got some affirmation for this, I got praise for this, why don't I turn it into a comic? So I turned it into a zine, and Jordan Crane saw it and he's like, this is fucking amazing, man. I made it

with a color copy. Those were like a dollar fifty at Kinko's back then. I stole them and made these zines. I made like 50 of them. And I'd always sneak into Comic-Con as Jim Lee or Jason Shiga or Derek, any Asian, Ron Lim. I just figured,

you know, I got into comics not during the Stan Lee era. My first was McFarlane, Jim Lee, those guys. So when I heard Stan Lee is the guy who invented all this, I just thought that was a guy related to Jim Lee.

I thought he was Korean. I thought Stan Lee was Korean. And it wasn't until Wizard magazine that I knew what all their faces looked like. So I snuck into Comic-Con with a Jim Lee big press pass and set up in a small press area, and Jordan Crane saw that.
And he's like, this is fucking unbelievable. And it was so shitty, because it was Xeroxed and glued together with a glue stick, cut with scissors and Sharpie marker.
And he's like, I'm going to print this in my thing. He had an anthology called Non. It was Brian Ralph, Jordan, all these guys. And I was like, oh, I feel like I belong.

I felt like part of something. My experience with comics was tunnel vision, GI Joe. That was it. I had GI Joe action figures, I shoplifted GI Joe action figures. I'd get the GI Joe comic for 75 cents back then, just get the GI Joe comic

from the spin rack at 7-Eleven, or I'd go to the Golden Apple that doesn't exist anymore, on Pico. I'd ride my bike there, and it was overwhelming. I'd walk in and see the Batman and the X-Men and everything, but I'd just go, is the new GI Joe out? And if it

wasn't, I'd just ride back home. It was just GI Joe and Garbage Pail Kids, that was my life, until the fucking Venom McFarlane cover, and the Wolverine, you know, claws with the Hulk reflection. I remember walking in slow motion being like, why are there so many fucking lines on this guy's face? It did something to me. It was almost

exactly like the first time I saw pornography. My head exploded. I go, I don't know who this Spider-Man is, but he's black and muscular and has fangs, and I'm like, oh man. And so I got into superhero comics from GI Joe that

way. And I always remember Golden Apple because they had the expensive comics up on the wall. I remember seeing Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles first print, or first or second printing, and it was like 300, 400 bucks, and that blew my mind, because I'm a kid

who could barely get scrounged 75 cents for a GI Joe. And it looked like newsprint. I asked the guy, what is that? You guys remember that time? It was Cold Blooded Chameleon Commandos, Adolescent Radioactive Black Belt Hamsters, everyone was ripping it off. There were

teenage samurai hamsters and gophers, everyone tried it, and they were on their seventh printing. And I remember looking at that wall as a little kid, probably eight or nine, being like, fuck, man, I hope I can get on that wall one day, make something

printed and have it go on a wall like that. That would be so amazing. So after Non came out with Jordan... David, can I ask you, I know this is great, but I have a question about the aesthetics of Slow Jams and a lot of your

comics from Non and other places. You do a lettering thing that's very much like you described, paste-up. I assume you're printing those out and then cutting up your lines of text and assembling them on a page somehow.
Where does that come from? Because that seems like more of a zine technique than what I'd see in a lot of comics at the time.

I'll just start by saying I fucking hate talking about art, because then it sounds like... whatever, I'm just gonna say it. I would see the best example of comic book lettering, or inking, like Charles Burns, and it would just blow me away. Or even Jordan Crane. When I'd see his originals...

And something happened to me when I was a kid, which is: you can't be left-handed. I know they say left-handed people are more creative, but as a Korean it's like bad luck or something. So my grandma and my mom and dad, they'd notice I grabbed for things with my left hand, and they'd wrap my hand in Saran Wrap, and I'd

chew it off. I don't know if any other left-handers out there would relate. Either of you left-handed? No. No. So you write left to right in America, right? So I'd sit down to draw as a kid, and I'd have the picture in my mind of a

perfect kind of drawing, and I'd be hand-lettering it, and it would be perfect, and at the last minute, because I'm going this way, I'd smudge it. I'd be like, fuck, man. And you can imagine later in life how liberating it was to see a Bill Sienkiewicz, because

I'm like, okay, cool, it doesn't have to be clean. But in my mind a good drawing meant clean lines. And I saw an episode where you were redrawing Spawn pages and stuff like that. That's me. So I have an ability, my mutant special power is I can see

anything, from a McFarlane to Charles Burns or Dan Clowes or Adrian Tomine, it doesn't matter. I can study it and then I can do it. I guess that sounds like bragging, but I'm just telling you what I can do. I can ape any style, I can draw in

any style, and the thing is it takes me a long time and it's fucking boring. So when I sit down to letter Slow Jams, I'm like, this is what I think it should look like, these are the comics I like, and then I start writing it and I get so bored, and I have to keep up with

the... I have all the classic artist symptoms. I have ADD, I'm bipolar, I have all those things. So picture me writing it with my little artist supplies, my little pen, and I'll add to that: Slow Jams is this story about

just unrequited stalking passion. It's a creepy book, and the first half of it I wasn't in a relationship, I'd never had a girlfriend, and then the second half I had a girlfriend, and it was super weird because I didn't know how to be a boy. I was like 23 at the time, I didn't know how to be in an adult relationship,

and she'd want to spend time with me, she'd go, 'what are you drawing over there,' and she'd come look, and she's like, 'I'm a real human girl that wants to fuck you and spend time with you, and you're drawing a comic about being obsessed with another girl.' And that's why

I meet other artists later and they're like, 'that's amazing how Slow Jams starts drawn really well and then it gets shittier to the pace of the story, it's genius how you did that.' And I go, no, I was living with a crazy bitch at the time and she was begging me,

so I'd rush through it. I know that's a really long answer to your question. I just do things and then people go, 'oh, was that a design choice?' But for me, my ADD or whatever you want to call it, maybe there's a page out

there somewhere where it's lettered perfectly and then I just lost interest, and I was like, you know what, I already wrote the story out, why don't I just fucking cut it out. So my impatience, my character defect of not being a patient person, is pretty

much... I mean, that's a great question, Jim, because it extends to why I never did comics at all after Slow Jams. I mention it too because I found Slow Jams in 2000. It was reviewed in the Comics Journal, they'd do their annual best-of issues, best

of 1999, and it was a relatively small list, almost a consensus, but several people named Slow Jams as their favorite comic. I was lucky to find it at Phantom of the Attic in Oakland, and it really spoke to me. But aesthetically you did a lot
in that comic that I had not seen before in comics. It expanded my landscape as to, like, this looks cool, why don't people do this? And it kind of gave me permission and some ideas of my own.

So I'm interested in that part and some of the aesthetic choices, because it did look different. I had never even heard the word 'mixed media' until I got to art school. And when I listen to you guys, I'm coming fresh off the Mark Millar interview,
and I go, what is this thing? We're fucking grown men right now talking, you guys got boxes of comics, why do people keep coming back to comics? And I'm like, because you can fucking do anything.

You can fucking do anything. It's literally the last frontier. And so as a lost kid during that age, in my early 20s, my late teens, just being lost and skating around LA doing graffiti, and knowing I can draw, that was the one area where people go, 'oh, he's not that good at school, he

doesn't know how to play sports, he's not good at getting girls, but man, when he draws...' I was like, but what does that mean? Because I love comic books, it's my favorite art form, I love graffiti, and that's not a real job until I turned it into one.
And then the pressure of being a first-generation immigrant, or son of immigrants: we escaped war, we got on a fucking boat and came here so you can be a graffiti artist? And coupled with what
you're saying, the LA riots and the racism, like, 'fuck you, you gook, you chink.' It wasn't like I grew up with people... that's not true. I did get beat up once.
[wry] Thanks, I pushed that one back into the memory. But it was hard, it was very difficult. And so I said, well, here's the one place where I can find positivity.
And I went to my first Comic-Con in San Diego. I was 19 or 20, something like that. And I saw my first original comic book pages with the whiteout, and I was like, oh fuck, that's what it looks like?

And there was a giant piece, I don't know how they split up the art chores, but it was Jon J Muth and Kent Williams, Havok and Wolverine: Meltdown. And it's Wolverine with this kind of hair, and his forms are like Popeye forms, and I was like, hell yeah, fuck yeah.
I'd never seen a comic book like that. I was like, what is that? That looks... And I was like, you can do that.
A lot of times in life you just need someone else to give you permission, right? Like, you can do that. And I was like, that looks so shitty and awesome at the same time.
And literally the same week that had an effect on me. I was back in LA, I had my black portfolio case, and I was a very, very angry yet very cocky kid. So I rode my skateboard

down La Brea and I went into every art gallery trying to show my stuff, and it was rejection, rejection, rejection. And then I skated into this gallery that's not there anymore called the Mary Karnowski Gallery, Kent Williams solo show. So I had just seen his art in San Diego, complete nerd-out, and this is when there were no women at Comic-Con,

and now I'm at this Kent Williams solo show opening, and it's exactly the same style of painting but no Wolverine. It's like Egon Schiele, this kind of shit, and I'm like, twenty thousand dollars for a painting? And I talked to him for a second,
and he had women around him and fancy Hollywood people, and I was like, you can do both? He's like, yeah, why not? And I was like, oh my God, this is amazing.
And so, this is my aesthetic coming out from these kinds of things, like, why not? My interest in art is so vast.

I love comics, I love graffiti, I love fine art, I love abstract art, I love it all. So, and this is later, getting into the more independent indie stuff, but I was like, there's things I've seen in TV shows,

things I've seen in... my first masturbation scene I ever saw was in There's Something About Mary, when he jerks off before. I had never seen that in a movie before, and that was literally roll-on-the-floor laughing.

I remember falling into the aisle, and I was like, that guy has cum in his hair. Right now nobody cares, right? All those movies that came out, American Pie, that was shocking because it had not touched that.
But in comics, when you get Johnny Ryan or Ivan Brunetti or Joe Matt, it's just like, what? You know, Robert Crumb. It's the last...
It feels to me... [getting emotional] sorry, I'm getting a little stuck right now, because I'm remembering the feelings I had at that age,

of going to a Comic-Con and seeing those pages in real life, the actual original pages, and knowing my skill level, I'm like, fuck, I could paint like that, it would just take me the next seven years. And I'd start to

meet, oh, that's what Jim Lee looks like, that's what this is. And I'd meet my favorite comic book artists and they all had this horrible hunchback, and they'd look like a Bernie Wrightson drawing. And I was like, I know I can do that, I just don't know if I have the patience to do that.
It takes... I can appreciate comics and the people who take 10 years to do one comic and all that, but I felt like, not to keep harping on the jerk-off scene from Slow Jams which people liked,
I just had so many ideas that I wanted to get out. And the thing, not to keep harping on the LA riots, is I thought I was going to die. I thought I was going to die.
And people go, oh, and then you didn't die and you move on. But that's not my understanding of how trauma works. Trauma stays with you. So anytime after that, I started hitchhiking,

I started putting myself in really dangerous situations. I went to Africa, I went to the Gaza Strip, because I was like, gopher broke every time. And that led to me being a really sick gambler and all these things.

But that's why when I put out a piece of work, I'm less interested in it looking perfect. Whereas I'd meet my favorite artists, I'd go to James Jean's house as a fan and be like, whoa, dude, those paintings don't even look like a human did them, and then I

look at a sketchbook and I'm like, this is way better. And I'm like, wait, if I like artists' imperfect, sketchy, fast shit, I'm just gonna guess most people would like that over the rendered stuff. Because I'd have one page in Slow Jams that I'd render, and I'm

like, it's gonna take me forever, and you sort of lose the energy of what I was feeling. I was literally trying to draw at the pace of myself thinking. And, I mean, talk about delusions of grandeur, I had Jordan Crane, who I was like, man, this guy is fucking
awesome, and then to hear about the Xeric Grant with Peter Laird, it was full circle. I was like, man, I used to be a kid looking at that Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles,
and that's the guy funding my comic. And the thing was, I didn't get it. I applied and I didn't get it, and I was heartbroken, because in my mind I was like, oh man, I'm so fucking cool,
I'm dope. And then I remember getting the rejection letter. And a friend of mine just said, well, why don't you try it again? And I was like, what do you mean?
He's like, you didn't get it this time, try it again next year. How many comic book artists do you think are out there? I had a friend who tried five times and got it.
And so I got it the next year, and it was Scott McCloud on the jury. And things started moving quickly. I remember I didn't know anything about printing or distribution.
And the way it works is if you win the Xeric Grant, they pick three or four guys, you get five grand, and you just send them the pay stubs and they cover it.

But I didn't know anything. So I said, can you guys just send me the five grand, and I promise you I won't spend it on drugs and whores, I'll definitely do it. And they're like, Dave, it doesn't really work that way. And they gave me some resources,

here's Quebecor Printing, and here's a list. And I was like, you guys don't understand, I'm a fucked-up person, I'm very disorganized. And I wrote this long letter, I swear on my fucking life, just give me the money. I sounded like a drug addict, and I promise you
I'll spend it on the comics. And I did. So I got the check, ordered the books, and had Jordan help me lay it out.
It was the different color inks. And then it shows up and I have, I think, 3,000 copies of Slow Jams in boxes in my house as furniture. I take five to Golden Apple,
I'm like, can you guys sell this? I took some of the guys at Meltdown, he's like, yeah, I'll take two. And I'm like, okay, seven down. I didn't know how to market a book like that.
So I started just sending it to magazines. I sent it to Rolling Stone, I'd find out who the art director is, for two things: to try to get illustration work, and to see if they'd write a review.
And then this woman, Claudine Ko, who worked at Jane magazine at the time, wrote a blurb this big of, like, 'this punk-rock skate graffiti kid did this comic, and it's the best thing ever.'

And all of a sudden I was getting all these letters from women, and I'd be going to the post office every day to send one copy, one copy, one copy. And that year, what's the Comic-Con in Bethesda? SPX.

Right, SPX. So I got invited to SPX, and I was being nominated for best newcomer comic book artist, or something like that. And I was new to this world, and in my mind as a young person I was like, man, I'm a fucking pimp, I got the Xeric Grant, that's my hero Peter Laird, Scott McCloud was on the fucking jury,

that's the guy who writes about comics and he's saying I'm the chosen one. And then I get there and I meet Neil Gaiman, and he's the speaker, and he's like, yeah, I gave him a copy, this is amazing. And then, talk about holding a grudge: that year it was best newcomer artist,

David Choe for Slow Jams, Craig Thompson for Goodbye, Chunky Rice, and Frank Cho for Liberty Meadows, who to this day everyone still thinks I'm related to. And every fucking person there was like, dude, this is the best fucking thing. And I was taking it in as this fucking weird

reject kid that had nothing good happen to him his whole life, and everyone's starting to tell me, you're the guy, you're the one. I was like, I'm gonna win this shit. And then the winner that year for best is Frank Cho. And who's on the jury? Frank Cho. I'm like, what the fuck is that about? But I let it go.

And I've never met the guy, I'm sure he's nice, he does some good Avengers work. But yeah, I just thought I was gonna be the guy. I have a really good Jim Lee story, because as Image formed, when I was a kid, I just kept drawing Spawn.
I just drew the fucking cape, and I'm gonna out-McFarlane McFarlane. Oh, how does a human being... the chains, the gravity, the proportions. And I was like, I'm gonna go next level,
and I made the cape, and I'm sitting in line, getting to express all the anger and fear and all those emotions you have as a teenage boy in Spawn's chains and his capes.
I'm drawing the craziest shit, waiting in line at Golden Apple for the Todd signing. It's the introduction of Image, Spawn is the flagship title.
There's a line snaking around like 10 blocks, there's police, there's helicopters, I'd never seen anything like it. Everyone in line was part of this comics tribe.
'Hey, look at what that fucking kid's doing over there.' And I was like, yeah, motherfucker. I'm drawing Spawn. And because of Wizard magazine, I knew what Jim Lee looked like.
I knew what he looked like. So a car pulls up and I see this guy with a baseball cap come out and start walking. Fuck, that's Jim Lee. And I go, hey bro, can you hold the line for me?
He's like, yeah, yeah, yeah. So I take my comic because I want to go show him, and I run up to him, and no one's bothering him, he's got his hat low.
And I say, hey Jim, look at my Spawn drawing. And he's like, oh man, that's pretty good. And then some kid in the back goes, 'that's fucking Jim Lee!' And he just gets mobbed.

And I was like, this is my introduction to... I didn't understand this was a special moment. I thought being a comic book artist was like being a rock star, even though that had never occurred before.

And he got mobbed and secured, like he was Elvis, like a Beatle, they put the thing around him. And at that moment I was like, fuck, I know what I've got to do in this life. I've got to be a comic book artist. I've got to be like Kent Williams, Jim Lee. I had all these different influences.

And yeah, it was crazy. So I did the one comic book. In 1999 is when I left LA, because I did one last mural on Sunset and Fountain, and I remember getting a call. I'm telling you these stories because I'm trying to put you guys in

the mindset of how things unfolded, to just do your first comic and then get nominated for best new thing. And I remember getting a call from a woman named Mira, who was, I think, Jae Lee's girlfriend at the time, and an editor at Marvel. And she said,

you know, I heard about this comic Slow Jams, and I heard you're not really a comic book artist, you're more like a graffiti artist. And I said, yeah, I do all those things. And she goes, we're thinking of doing a more adult, street-contemporary version of the X-Men called NYX.

And I said, okay. And she's like, would you be interested in doing the art for that? And I was like, fuck, I ain't even fucking trying and these fuckers are coming. I'm getting X-Men. I was like 21 at the time. I'm like, everything's lining up for me, my
